statement: Ana and Ben have 15 marbles together. Ben and Cal have 12 marbles together. Ana and Cal have 13 marbles together. How many marbles do the three children have altogether?

choices.misconception: I worked out how many marbles Ana has and stopped before adding Ben's and Cal's.
I used only Ana and Ben's total and left Cal out.
I added the two totals with Ana in them, 15 and 13, but that counts Ana two times.
I added all three totals, but that counts every child two times.

hints: Draw a bar for each child. Which two bars make the 15?
Draw each total as a pair of bars: Ana with Ben, Ben with Cal, Ana with Cal. Put all three pairs together and count how many times each child's bar appears.
15 + 12 + 13 = 40. In those three pairs, Ana, Ben and Cal each appear two times.

solutions.reliable: Put the three pairs together: 15 + 12 + 13 = 40. Each child is in exactly two of the pairs, so 40 counts everyone two times. Half of 40 is 20, so the three children have 20 marbles. Check: Ana has 8, Ben has 7 and Cal has 5, and 8 + 7 = 15, 7 + 5 = 12, 8 + 5 = 13. The idea to keep: when every part is counted twice, halve the total.
solutions.elegant: Ana and Cal have 13 and Ben and Cal have 12. Both pairs have Cal, so Ana has 1 more than Ben. Ana and Ben have 15, so Ben has 7 and Ana has 8. Then Cal has 12 take away 7, which is 5. Altogether 8 + 7 + 5 = 20. The idea to keep: two totals that share a person show the difference between the other two.

whyOnTest: Bar models for part and whole show that each child appears in two of the totals, which is why adding all three totals counts everyone twice.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
